lessons.title: The shell and commands
lessons.intro: A shell is a program that reads what you type and runs other programs for you. Nearly every server is managed through one. This module covers what a command is made of, how to find out what a command does, and how a command reports success or failure.

steps.title: What a shell is
steps.text:
Three words get mixed up.

- A **terminal** is the window that shows text and takes your typing.
- A **shell** is the program running inside it that reads each line and acts on it.
- A **command** is one line you give the shell, usually the name of a program and some instructions for it.

The most common shell on Linux is **Bash**. This course uses it. Other shells, such as Zsh, behave the same for everything here unless stated.

A shell waits, showing a **prompt**. You type a line and press Enter. The shell runs it, shows any output and prints the prompt again.

steps.title: The parts of a command
steps.text:
A command line is a list of words separated by spaces. The first word is the program to run. The rest are passed to that program.

Those remaining words are of two kinds.

- **Options** (also called flags) change how the program behaves. They start with a dash.
- **Arguments** say what the program should act on, such as a file name.


Short options are one dash and one letter, and several can be joined: `ls -la` means `ls -l -a`. Long options are two dashes and a word. Many options have both forms, and `-a` and `--all` are the same thing.

Some options take a value: `head -n 20 file.txt` shows the first 20 lines.

Linux is case-sensitive. `ls` and `LS` are different names, and so are `Notes.txt` and `notes.txt`.

steps.title: Spaces separate words
steps.text:
Since a space ends a word, a file name with a space in it is read as two arguments. Wrap such a name in quotes, or put a backslash before the space.


This is the cause of a great many confusing errors. Quoting is covered properly in the module on variables.

steps.title: Finding out what a command does
steps.text:
Nobody remembers every option. The system documents itself, and using that documentation is a normal part of working.

- `man ls` opens the **manual page** for a command. Move with the arrow keys or the space bar, search by typing `/` and a word, and leave with `q`.
- `ls --help` prints a short summary of options, for most commands.
- `type ls` says what kind of thing a name is, and where the program lives.

A manual page is a reference. It is dense. Read the one-line description at the top, then search inside it for the word you need.

steps.title: Which word is which
steps.text: Look at this command: `tail -n 50 -f /var/log/app.log`

steps.title: Moving around the line
steps.text:
A few keys save a great deal of typing.

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Tab | Completes a command or file name. Press twice to list the choices |
| Up and Down | Step through earlier commands |
| Ctrl+R | Search the history as you type |
| Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E | Jump to the start or end of the line |
| Ctrl+C | Stop the running command |
| Ctrl+L | Clear the screen |
| Ctrl+D | End input. At an empty prompt, this logs you out |

Use Tab constantly. It is faster, and it catches mistakes: if a name does not complete, it probably does not exist.

`history` lists the commands you have run. Be aware that anything typed on a command line is saved there, which is one reason never to type a password as part of a command.

steps.title: Success and failure
steps.text:
Every program ends by returning a number to the shell, called its **exit status** (or exit code).

- `0` means success.
- Any other number, from 1 to 255, means some kind of failure. The meaning of each number depends on the program.

The shell keeps the status of the last command in a special variable, `$?`.


The exit status is how scripts and other programs know whether a step worked. It matters more than the text on the screen. A program can print a message and still succeed, or print nothing and fail.

steps.title: Chain commands on their result
steps.text:
The shell can decide whether to run a command from the status of the one before.

- `a && b` runs `b` only if `a` succeeded.
- `a || b` runs `b` only if `a` failed.
- `a ; b` runs `b` afterwards, whatever happened.


The difference between `&&` and `;` is important. `cd /tmp/work ; rm -rf *` deletes everything in whatever directory you are in if the `cd` fails. With `&&`, the delete does not run.

steps.title: Chained with a semicolon
steps.text: Someone types `cd /srv/app/cache ; rm -rf *` to clear a cache. The directory `/srv/app/cache` does not exist, and their current directory is `/srv/app`.

steps.title: Reading an error message
steps.text:
When a command fails, it usually says why, in a fixed shape: the program's name, what it was acting on, and the reason.

| Message | Usually means |
| --- | --- |
| `command not found` | No program of that name on this system, or a typing error |
| `No such file or directory` | The path is wrong, or you are in a different directory from the one you think |
| `Permission denied` | The file exists and your user may not do this to it |
| `Is a directory` | You gave a directory to a command that wants a file |
| `Not a directory` | Part of the path is a file |

Read the whole message before trying again. Most of them say exactly what is wrong.

steps.title: Exercise: read the commands
steps.text:
For each line, name the program, the options and the arguments. Say what you expect it to do, using only what this module covered, and say how you would find out the rest.

1. `ls -lh /var/log`
2. `cp -r "Project Files" backup`
3. `grep -i error app.log && echo found`
4. `mkdir reports ; cd reports`
5. `sort -n -r scores.txt`

Then say what is risky about line 4, and rewrite it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Program** `ls`. **Options** `-l` and `-h`, joined. **Argument** `/var/log`. It lists that directory in long format. What `-h` does is not something this module covered. `man ls` or `ls --help` says that it prints sizes in readable units such as K and M.
2. **Program** `cp`. **Option** `-r`. **Arguments** `Project Files` and `backup`. The quotes make the first name one argument, though it contains a space. It copies something to `backup`. The manual says `-r` copies a directory and everything in it.
3. **Program** `grep`, with the option `-i` and two arguments: the word to look for and the file. Then `&&` runs `echo found` only if `grep` succeeded. `grep` succeeds when it finds a match, so "found" is printed only when the word is in the file.
4. Two commands. `mkdir` makes a directory, and then `cd` enters it.
5. **Program** `sort`, with options `-n` and `-r` and one argument. The manual says `-n` sorts by number and `-r` reverses, so the largest number comes first.

**Line 4.** With a semicolon, `cd reports` runs even if `mkdir` failed. Here that is mostly harmless: `cd` fails too, or enters an older directory of the same name. The habit is what is dangerous, since the next command in such a chain may delete or overwrite. Write `mkdir reports && cd reports`, so the second step depends on the first.

lessons.title: Files and directories
lessons.intro: Everything on a Linux system is arranged in one tree of directories. This module covers how to read a path, how to move around, and how to create, copy, move and delete files without losing any.

steps.title: One tree
steps.text:
Linux has a single directory tree. It starts at the **root directory**, written `/`. Every file and every directory sits somewhere beneath it. There are no drive letters. A second disk or a USB stick appears as a directory somewhere in the same tree.

A few directories have the same purpose on every system.

| Directory | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `/home` | Each user's own files, in `/home/<name>` |
| `/etc` | System-wide configuration files |
| `/var` | Data that changes: logs in `/var/log`, databases, caches |
| `/tmp` | Temporary files, removed at restart |
| `/usr` | Installed programs and libraries |
| `/bin`, `/sbin` | Essential commands |
| `/opt` | Software installed separately from the system's packages |
| `/root` | The administrator's home directory |
| `/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys` | Not real files. Windows onto devices and the running system |

Knowing these saves time. A configuration file is nearly always under `/etc`, and a log under `/var/log`.

steps.title: Paths
steps.text:
A **path** says where a file is. There are two kinds.

An **absolute path** starts at the root, so it begins with `/`. It means the same thing wherever you are: `/home/ana/notes.txt`.

A **relative path** starts from the directory you are in, called the **working directory**. It does not begin with `/`: `projects/site`.

Three short names help.

- `.` is the current directory.
- `..` is the parent directory, one level up.
- `~` is your home directory.


Most "No such file or directory" errors come from a relative path used from the wrong directory. When unsure, run `pwd`.

steps.title: Listing
steps.text:
`ls` lists a directory. Its long format shows what each entry is.


A name that starts with a dot is **hidden**. `ls` leaves it out unless you add `-a`. Hidden files are mostly configuration, such as `.bashrc`. They are not protected in any way. They are only out of sight.

Useful options: `-l` long format, `-a` include hidden, `-h` readable sizes, `-t` newest first, `-r` reverse the order.

steps.title: Which directory
steps.text: A user's working directory is `/home/ana/projects`. They run `cd ../../bilal/docs`.

steps.title: Creating
steps.text: Without `-p`, `mkdir data/2025/march` fails if `data/2025` does not exist. With it, the whole chain is created, and an existing directory is not an error. That makes `mkdir -p` the form to use in scripts.

steps.title: Copying and moving
steps.text:
`cp` copies. `mv` moves, and it is also how a file is renamed.


Both overwrite an existing destination without asking. Copying `a.txt` onto `b.txt` replaces `b.txt`, and its old contents are gone. Add `-i` to be asked first, or `-n` to never overwrite. On recent systems `cp -n` still works and prints a warning that suggests the newer spelling, `--update=none`.

A trailing slash on a destination, as in `reports/`, makes your meaning clear: this is a directory to put things in. Without it, if `reports` does not exist, `mv ideas.txt reports` renames the file to `reports`.

steps.title: Deleting
steps.text:
`rm` deletes files. There is no recycle bin. A deleted file is gone.


`rm -r` removes a whole tree. With `-f` added, it also suppresses every question and error. `rm -rf` followed by the wrong path is the classic way to destroy a system or a project.

Habits that prevent it:

- Run `ls` with the same path first, and look at what it matches.
- Never run `rm -rf` on a path built from a variable that might be empty. `rm -rf "$DIR/"` with `DIR` unset becomes `rm -rf /`.
- Prefer moving things to a holding directory, and delete later.
- Do not use `sudo` for a delete unless you must.

steps.title: Wildcards
steps.text:
The shell expands certain characters into a list of matching file names before the command runs. This is called **globbing**.

| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `*` | Any run of characters, including none |
| `?` | Exactly one character |
| `[abc]` | One of the listed characters |
| `[0-9]` | One character in the range |

`*.log` matches every name ending in `.log`. `report-202?.csv` matches `report-2024.csv` and `report-2025.csv`.

The shell does the expansion, not the command. `rm *.log` becomes `rm a.log b.log c.log` before `rm` starts. So you can preview any pattern safely with `echo` or `ls`.

A `*` does not match hidden files, and a pattern that matches nothing is passed to the command unchanged.

steps.title: A space in the wrong place
steps.text: Someone means to delete every file ending in `.tmp` in the current directory. They type `rm -f * .tmp`, with a space after the star by mistake.

steps.title: Links
steps.text:
A **symbolic link** (symlink) is a small file that points at another path. Opening it opens the target.


Links are used to give a stable name to something that changes, such as "the current release". If the target is removed, the link stays and points at nothing. That is a broken link, and opening it reports "No such file or directory" although `ls` shows the link.

steps.title: Exercise: tidy a directory
steps.text:
Your working directory is `/home/ana/work`. It contains:

```text
draft v1.txt   draft v2.txt   final.txt   notes.md
img1.png  img2.png  img10.png
old/          (a directory with 300 files)
.env          (a hidden file)
```

Write the commands for each task. Preview anything destructive first.

1. Make a directory `images` and move the three PNG files into it.
2. Make `archive/2025/drafts`, and move the two drafts there.
3. Copy `final.txt` to `final.bak`, without overwriting an existing backup.
4. Delete the `old` directory.
5. Say whether `rm *` would remove `.env`, and whether `img?.png` matches all three images.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Notes**

- In task 1, `&&` means nothing is moved if the directory could not be made. The trailing slash on `images/` means that, if the directory were missing, `mv` would fail and not rename a file to `images`.
- In task 2, the names contain spaces, so they are quoted. The pattern `draft*.txt` also works, since the shell passes each matched name as one argument, spaces included.
- In task 3, a recent system prints a warning for `cp -n` and still does the right thing. `cp --update=none` is the newer spelling, and older systems do not have it.
- In task 4, plain `rm -r` is enough. Adding `-f` gains nothing here and removes the warnings that could save you.

**Task 5.** `rm *` does not remove `.env`, since `*` does not match hidden files. And `img?.png` matches `img1.png` and `img2.png` only. The `?` stands for exactly one character, and `img10.png` has two there. Use `img*.png`.

lessons.title: Read and search files
lessons.intro: Most work on a server is reading: a configuration file, a log, the output of a command. This module covers the tools for looking at text, for finding lines inside files, and for finding files by name, size or age.

steps.title: Looking at a file
steps.text:
Several commands show a file's contents. Which one fits depends on the file's size.

| Command | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `cat file` | A short file. Prints all of it at once |
| `less file` | A long file. Shows one screen at a time |
| `head file` | The first 10 lines |
| `tail file` | The last 10 lines |
| `wc -l file` | How many lines it has |

Running `cat` on a 2 GB log floods the terminal. Check the size first with `ls -lh` or `wc -l`, and use `less` for anything long.

steps.title: Using less
steps.text:
`less` is the tool you will use most for reading, so its keys are worth learning.

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Space, `b` | Forward and back one screen |
| `g`, `G` | Jump to the start, jump to the end |
| `/word` | Search forward for a word |
| `?word` | Search backward |
| `n`, `N` | Next match, previous match |
| `F` | Follow the file as it grows. Ctrl+C stops following |
| `q` | Quit |

`less` does not load the whole file, so it opens a huge log at once. Manual pages are shown with it, which is why the same keys work there.

steps.title: Watching a file grow
steps.text:
Logs are written continuously. `tail -f` prints the end of a file and then keeps printing new lines as they arrive, until you press Ctrl+C.


This is the usual way to watch what a service does while you send it a request from another terminal.

steps.title: Searching inside files
steps.text:
`grep` prints the lines of a file that match a pattern. It is the most used search tool on Linux.


`-A`, `-B` and `-C` show the lines around each match. An error message is usually explained by the lines just before and after it.

`grep` also sets its exit status: 0 when something matched, 1 when nothing did. That makes it usable as a test in scripts.

steps.title: Patterns
steps.text:
The pattern `grep` takes is a **regular expression**: a small language for describing text. A few pieces cover most needs.

| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `abc` | Those characters |
| `.` | Any one character |
| `^` | The start of a line |
| `$` | The end of a line |
| `[0-9]` | One digit |
| `[a-z]` | One lower-case letter |
| `*` | The item before it, zero or more times |
| `\.` | A real dot |

Add `-E` for the extended syntax, which also has `+` (one or more), `?` (optional), `|` (or) and `( )` for grouping.

Put the pattern in single quotes. Characters such as `*`, `$` and `|` mean something to the shell as well, and without quotes the shell changes them before `grep` sees them.


`-F` treats the pattern as plain text. It is the safe choice when you are searching for something that contains dots or other special characters and want no surprises.

steps.title: What matches
steps.text: A file contains these four lines: `error: disk full`, `no errors found`, `ERROR: timeout`, and `warning: slow`. Someone runs `grep '^error' file`.

steps.title: Finding files
steps.text:
`grep` looks inside files. `find` looks for the files themselves, by walking a directory tree and testing each entry.


The shape is always `find <where> <tests>`. Tests are combined with "and" by default. `-type f` means files, and `-type d` means directories.

Quote the name pattern. Without quotes, the shell expands `*.conf` against the current directory before `find` runs, and the search is then for the wrong thing.

steps.title: Acting on what find returns
steps.text:
`find` can run a command on each result.


`{}` stands for the file found. Ending with `\;` runs the command once per file, and ending with `+` passes many files to one run, which is faster.

Always run the search with `-print` before adding `-delete`. The tests decide what is destroyed, and a mistake in one cannot be undone.

steps.title: Files that are not text
steps.text:
Some files are not meant to be read as text: images, archives, compiled programs. Printing one to the terminal shows garbage and can leave the terminal in an odd state. The command `reset` restores it.

`file` tells you what something is, by looking at its contents and not at its name.


Compressed logs are common. `zcat`, `zless` and `zgrep` work like `cat`, `less` and `grep` on `.gz` files without unpacking them first.

steps.title: Comparing two files
steps.text:
`diff` shows the lines that differ between two files. It is how you find out what changed in a configuration file.


In the `-u` format, a line starting with `-` is only in the first file, and one starting with `+` is only in the second. Lines with neither are unchanged context.

steps.title: Unquoted pattern
steps.text: In a directory that contains `app.conf` and `db.conf`, someone runs `find /etc -name *.conf` without quotes.

steps.title: Exercise: investigate a log
steps.text:
A web server writes one line per request to `/var/log/web/access.log`, about 3 million lines a day. Each line has the client address, the time, the request and a status code, such as:

```text
203.0.113.9 [04/Mar/2025:14:02:11] "GET /api/orders/88 HTTP/1.1" 500 0.841
```

Write a command for each task.

1. Find out how large the file is and how many lines it has, without printing it.
2. Show the last 50 lines.
3. Watch new requests arrive.
4. Count how many requests returned status 500.
5. Show the requests to `/api/orders` that did not return 200.
6. Find every `.gz` file in `/var/log/web` that is over 30 days old, and list them with their sizes.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Notes**

- In tasks 4 and 5, the pattern includes the quote and the spaces around the number. Plain `grep 500` would also match a response time of `0.500`, an address containing 500 and order number 5001. Anchor a pattern to what surrounds the value you mean.
- Task 5 joins two commands with `|`, which passes the output of the first to the second. That is the subject of the next module. The first `grep` keeps the order requests, and the second removes the successful ones.

lessons.title: Pipes and redirection
lessons.intro: Linux commands are small tools that each do one job. Their power comes from joining them. This module covers the three streams every program has, how to send them to files, and how to feed the output of one command into the next.

steps.title: Three streams
steps.text:
Every program starts with three channels already open.

| Stream | Number | Normally connected to | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard input (stdin) | 0 | The keyboard | Data the program reads |
| Standard output (stdout) | 1 | The terminal | The program's results |
| Standard error (stderr) | 2 | The terminal | Error messages and diagnostics |

Both outputs appear on the same screen, so they look like one. They are separate, and that separation is useful. The results of a command can be saved to a file or passed to another program while its error messages still reach you.

A program does not know or care what its streams are connected to. The shell sets them up before the program starts. Redirection and pipes are the shell connecting those streams to something else.

steps.title: Sending output to a file
steps.text:
`>` sends standard output to a file. `>>` does the same and adds to the end.


`>` replaces the file's contents. If the file exists, what it held is gone before the command even starts. `>>` keeps what is there. Mixing the two up is a common way to lose a file.

One trap follows from that. In `sort data.txt > data.txt`, the shell empties `data.txt` first, and then `sort` reads an empty file. Write to a different name and rename it afterwards.

steps.title: Errors are a separate stream
steps.text:
`>` moves only standard output. Error messages still go to the terminal.


To redirect standard error, name its number.


`2>&1` means "send stream 2 to wherever stream 1 is going now". The order matters: it must come after the redirection of stream 1.

`/dev/null` is a special file that discards everything written to it. Sending errors there hides them, which is occasionally what you want and often a way to hide the reason something failed.

steps.title: Where does it go
steps.text: A script runs `backup.sh > backup.log` every night. The backup has been failing for a week, and `backup.log` is empty each morning.

steps.title: Reading input from a file
steps.text:
`<` connects a file to a program's standard input.


Many commands accept a file name as an argument too, so `sort names.txt` does the same as the first line. When no file is named, they read standard input. That behaviour is what makes pipes work.

steps.title: Pipes
steps.text:
A **pipe**, written `|`, connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next. The data passes straight from one program to the other without touching a file.


Any number of commands can be joined. Each one reads what the one before wrote, does its small job and passes the result on. A chain of them is called a **pipeline**.

The commands in a pipeline run at the same time. The first does not finish before the second starts. Data flows through as it is produced, so a pipeline can process a file far larger than memory.

steps.title: Only standard output goes down the pipe
steps.text:
A pipe carries standard output. Standard error skips it and goes to the terminal. That is usually what you want: errors are not mixed into the data being processed.

To send errors through the pipe as well, merge them first with `2>&1`.

steps.title: Save and show
steps.text: `tee` copies its input to a file and also passes it on. Use it to keep a record of output while still watching it.

steps.title: The exit status of a pipeline
steps.text:
The exit status of a pipeline is the status of its last command. The earlier ones are ignored.


`cat` failed, `wc` succeeded in counting nothing, and the pipeline reports success. A script that checks only the final status will carry on as if all were well.

In Bash, `set -o pipefail` changes this, so a pipeline fails if any command in it failed. Scripts should turn it on. The scripts module returns to it.

steps.title: Using output as arguments
steps.text:
A pipe gives a command data on its standard input. Sometimes you need the output of one command as the arguments of another. There are two ways.

**Command substitution** runs a command and puts its output into the command line.


**`xargs`** reads items from standard input and runs a command with them as arguments.


File names with spaces break the plain form, since `xargs` splits on spaces. The `-print0` and `-0` pair separates names with a null character, which cannot appear in a name. Use that pair whenever names come from `find`.

steps.title: Here documents
steps.text:
A **here document** feeds several lines of text to a command's standard input, written right in the command or script.


Everything up to the closing word is the input. Variables and command substitutions inside are expanded. Quote the opening word, as in `<<'EOF'`, to keep the text exactly as written.

steps.title: Which gets counted
steps.text: Someone wants to know how many errors a command prints, and runs `./check.sh | wc -l`. The command prints 40 error lines to standard error and 3 result lines to standard output.

steps.title: Exercise: build the pipelines
steps.text:
Write one command line for each task.

1. Run `./migrate.sh`, saving results and errors together in `migrate.log`, while also watching them.
2. Run `./cleanup.sh` so that its results are discarded and its errors are saved to `cleanup.err`.
3. Count how many files under `/etc` have names ending in `.conf`, hiding any "Permission denied" messages.
4. Show the 10 largest files in `/var/log`. `du -a /var/log` prints a size and a path for each file, and `sort -n` sorts by number.
5. Add a line with the current date and the text "backup started" to the end of `/var/log/backup.log`.
6. Explain what is wrong with `sort users.txt > users.txt`, and fix it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Notes**

- In task 1, `2>&1` comes before the pipe, so both streams enter it. `tee` then writes the file and shows the same text.
- In task 3, only the error stream is discarded. The list of names still goes down the pipe to be counted.
- In task 4, `sort -n` puts the largest last, so `tail` takes the final ten. `sort -n -r | head -n 10` is equally good.
- In task 5, `>>` is essential. `>` would wipe the log each time.
- In task 6, the shell empties `users.txt` before `sort` starts, so `sort` reads nothing and the file ends up empty. Writing to a second file and renaming it avoids that, and `&&` means the rename happens only if the sort succeeded. `sort -o users.txt users.txt` also works, since `sort` handles that case itself.

lessons.title: Process text
lessons.intro: Logs, configuration and command output are all lines of text. A handful of small tools, joined with pipes, can answer most questions about them. This module covers sorting, counting, picking out columns and changing text.

steps.title: Lines and fields
steps.text:
Text tools share one view of the world. Input is a series of **lines**. Each line may be split into **fields** by a separator: spaces, tabs, commas or colons.

Most of the work is a combination of four steps.

1. **Select** the lines you want (`grep`).
2. **Extract** the field you care about (`cut`, `awk`).
3. **Sort and count** (`sort`, `uniq`, `wc`).
4. **Change** text (`sed`, `tr`).

Build a pipeline one step at a time. Run the first command and look at the output. Add the next and look again. A long pipeline written in one go is hard to get right and harder to debug.

steps.title: Sorting
steps.text:
`sort` puts lines in order.


The default order is by character, not by value. As text, `10` comes before `9`, since `1` comes before `9`. Use `-n` whenever the lines are numbers.

`-t` sets the field separator and `-k` chooses the field to sort on.

steps.title: Counting repeats
steps.text:
`uniq` collapses neighbouring lines that are identical. It compares only lines that are next to each other, so its input must be sorted first.


The combination below is one of the most useful in all of shell work. It answers "what are the most common values?".

steps.title: Picking columns with cut
steps.text:
`cut` extracts fields from each line, given a separator.


`-d` sets the separator and `-f` names the fields. `cut` is strict: it splits on every single separator character. Columns padded with several spaces, as in the output of `ls -l` or `ps`, produce empty fields and wrong results. For those, use `awk`.

steps.title: Picking columns with awk
steps.text:
`awk` splits each line into fields on any run of spaces or tabs, and lets you print the ones you want. The fields are named `$1`, `$2` and so on. `$0` is the whole line, and `$NF` is the last field.


An `awk` program has the shape `condition { action }`. With no condition, the action runs for every line. With no action, matching lines are printed. `END { ... }` runs once after the last line.

`awk` is a complete language. The small part shown here, printing fields and filtering on them, covers most daily use. Put the program in single quotes, so the shell leaves `$1` alone.

steps.title: Top talkers
steps.text:
An access log has the client address as the first field of each line. Someone runs:

```bash
awk '{print $1}' access.log | uniq -c | sort -n -r | head -n 3
```

steps.title: Translating characters
steps.text:
`tr` replaces or deletes single characters. It reads standard input only.


The third line fixes a frequent problem. Text files made on Windows end each line with two characters, a carriage return and a line feed. Linux expects only the line feed. A script with Windows line endings fails with confusing errors such as `bad interpreter` or `command not found` for a command that plainly exists.

steps.title: Replacing text with sed
steps.text:
`sed` edits text as it flows past. Its most used command is substitution: `s/old/new/`.


`sed` prints the changed text and leaves the file alone. To change the file itself, add `-i`.


Editing in place has no undo. Run the command without `-i` first and read the output. When you do use `-i`, give it a suffix, as in `-i.bak`, so that a copy of the original is kept.

The "old" part is a regular expression, so characters such as `.` and `*` have special meaning there. `s/1.5/2.0/` also changes `105` and `1x5`, since the dot matches any character. Write `1\.5` for a real dot.

steps.title: Counting
steps.text: `wc` counts lines, words and bytes.

steps.title: Putting them together
steps.text:
A realistic question: which request paths produced the most server errors today?


Read it one step at a time: keep today's lines, keep the path of those with a status of 500 or more, group equal paths, count them, and put the largest first.

A backslash at the end of a line continues the command on the next line. It makes a long pipeline readable.

steps.title: When to stop
steps.text:
These tools are excellent for questions asked once at a terminal. They are a poor fit for some jobs.

- **Structured formats.** JSON, YAML and XML have rules that line-based tools do not understand. A value may span lines or contain the separator. Use a tool made for the format, such as `jq` for JSON.
- **CSV with quoted fields.** `"Smith, Ana",42` has a comma inside a field. `cut -d,` splits it in the wrong place.
- **Anything that will be kept and maintained.** A forty-line pipeline of `sed` and `awk` is hard to read and to test. When a one-off turns into a program, write it in a programming language.

steps.title: The dot
steps.text: A configuration file contains `version=1.5` and `timeout=105`. Someone runs `sed -i 's/1.5/2.0/g' app.conf` to update the version.

steps.title: Exercise: answer from the data
steps.text:
The file `/etc/passwd` has one line per user account, with fields separated by colons. The first field is the user name, the third is the numeric user ID, and the seventh is the user's shell:

```text
ana:x:1001:1001:Ana Ruiz:/home/ana:/bin/bash
```

An access log has lines in this form, with fields separated by spaces: the client address, the time, the method, the path, the status and the response size in bytes.

```text
203.0.113.9 14:02:11 GET /api/orders 200 5120
```

Write a pipeline for each question.

1. List all user names, sorted.
2. Show how many accounts use each shell, most common first.
3. Show the names of accounts whose user ID is 1000 or more.
4. Show the 5 client addresses that made the most requests.
5. Show the total number of bytes sent.
6. Print the log with every `/api/` path changed to `/v2/api/`, without changing the file.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Notes**

- In tasks 1 and 2, `cut` is right, since `/etc/passwd` uses exactly one colon between fields. For the access log, `awk` is the safer choice.
- Task 3 needs a numeric comparison on a field, which `cut` and `grep` cannot do. `awk` with `-F:` can.
- Task 4 is the standard counting pattern. The `sort` before `uniq -c` is what groups the addresses.
- In task 6, `|` is used as the separator in the `sed` command, since the text contains slashes. With `/` as the separator, every slash in the paths would need a backslash. There is no `-i`, so the file is untouched.

lessons.title: Users and permissions
lessons.intro: Every file belongs to a user and carries rules about who may read, change or run it. "Permission denied" is the most common error on Linux, and it always has a specific cause. This module covers how to read those rules, how to change them, and how administrator access works.

steps.title: Users and groups
steps.text:
Linux is a multi-user system. Every process runs as some **user**, and every file is owned by one.

A user has a name and a numeric ID. A **group** is a named set of users, used to give several people the same access. Each user has one primary group and may belong to others.

One user is special. **root**, with user ID 0, is the administrator. The permission rules do not apply to root. It can read, change and delete anything.

Many users are not people. Services run as their own accounts, such as `www-data` or `postgres`, so that a fault in one service cannot touch another's files.

steps.title: Reading permissions
steps.text:
`ls -l` shows the rules for each file in its first column.


There are three sets of three letters, for three classes of user.

- **Owner** (user): the user who owns the file.
- **Group**: members of the file's group.
- **Others**: everyone else.

In each set, `r` is read, `w` is write and `x` is execute. A dash means that permission is not given.

The system checks one class only, the first that applies. If you are the owner, the owner's set is used and the other two are ignored, even if they would allow more.

steps.title: What the letters mean
steps.text:
The three permissions mean different things for a file and for a directory. The directory meanings surprise people.

| | On a file | On a directory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `r` read | View the contents | List the names inside it |
| `w` write | Change the contents | Create, rename and delete entries in it |
| `x` execute | Run it as a program | Enter it, and reach the files inside |

Two consequences are worth learning by heart.

- **Deleting a file depends on the directory**, not on the file. To delete a file you need write permission on the directory that holds it. A file you cannot read or write can still be deleted by you if you can write to its directory.
- **To reach a file, you need `x` on every directory in its path.** A world-readable file inside a directory you cannot enter is unreachable.

steps.title: Numbers for permissions
steps.text:
Permissions are often written as three digits. Each digit is the sum of the values for one class: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1.

| Digit | Letters | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7 | `rwx` | 4 + 2 + 1 |
| 6 | `rw-` | 4 + 2 |
| 5 | `r-x` | 4 + 1 |
| 4 | `r--` | 4 |
| 0 | `---` | nothing |

So `644` is `rw-r--r--`: the owner reads and writes, and everyone else reads. `755` is `rwxr-xr-x`: the owner does anything, and everyone else may read and run.

| Mode | Typical use |
| --- | --- |
| `644` | Ordinary files |
| `755` | Programs, scripts and directories |
| `600` | Private files, such as keys |
| `700` | Private directories |
| `640` | Configuration with secrets, readable by a service's group |

steps.title: Changing permissions
steps.text:
`chmod` changes a file's permissions. It accepts numbers or letters.


In the letter form, `u` is the owner, `g` the group, `o` others and `a` all three. `+` adds, `-` removes and `=` sets exactly.

Only the owner of a file, or root, can change its permissions.

steps.title: Reading a mode
steps.text: A file is listed as `-rwxr-x--- 1 deploy ops 812 Mar 4 release.sh`. The user `ana` is a member of the group `ops`. The user `bilal` is not.

steps.title: Changing ownership
steps.text:
`chown` changes who owns a file, and `chgrp` changes its group. Changing a file's owner needs root.


A very common fault is a file owned by the wrong user. A service runs as `www-data` and cannot write to a directory owned by `root`. The fix is to give that one directory to the service's user. It is not to make it writable by everyone.

steps.title: Becoming root with sudo
steps.text:
Working as root all the time is dangerous, since one mistyped command can destroy the system. The normal arrangement is to log in as an ordinary user and use `sudo` to run single commands as root.


`sudo` asks for your own password, checks a rule file to see whether you are allowed, runs the command and records it in a log. Who did what as root can be traced.

Use it deliberately. If a command fails with "Permission denied", find out why before reaching for `sudo`. Often the right fix is a change of ownership or group. Running everything with `sudo` also creates files owned by root, which then cause permission errors for the ordinary user later.

One trap: `sudo` applies to the command, not to a redirection. In `sudo echo "x" > /etc/file`, the shell opens `/etc/file` as you, before `sudo` runs, and it fails. Use `echo "x" | sudo tee /etc/file`.

steps.title: Why 777 is the wrong fix
steps.text:
`chmod 777` gives read, write and execute to everyone. It makes "Permission denied" go away, which is why it is so often suggested. It does so by removing the protection entirely.

On a server, "everyone" includes every service account. If a web application is broken into, the attacker runs as its user. With correct permissions they can touch only that application's files. With 777 scattered about, they can change other applications, scripts that root runs, and configuration.

The correct approach is to find out which user needs access, and grant that user or its group the least that works.

1. Which user is the process running as? (`ps` shows it.)
2. Who owns the file, and what is its mode? (`ls -l`.)
3. Change the owner or group, or add one permission for that class.

steps.title: Defaults for new files
steps.text:
New files get their permissions from a setting called the **umask**, which removes permissions from the starting values. The usual umask, `022`, gives new files `644` and new directories `755`. A umask of `077` makes new files private, `600` and `700`.

You rarely change it. Knowing it exists explains why a file you created came out with the permissions it has.

steps.title: Three special bits
steps.text:
A few modes have a fourth digit or an unusual letter. You need to recognise them.

- **setuid** (`s` in the owner's execute position). The program runs as the file's owner, not as the user who started it. `passwd` is setuid root, so that an ordinary user can change their own password. A setuid root program with a flaw gives root access, so there should be very few.
- **setgid on a directory.** New files inside inherit the directory's group. Useful for shared project directories.
- **The sticky bit** (`t` on a directory). Only a file's owner may delete it, even though everyone can write to the directory. `/tmp` has it.

steps.title: Cannot write
steps.text: A deploy script runs as the user `deploy` and fails with "Permission denied" when writing to `/srv/app/releases`. `ls -ld /srv/app/releases` shows `drwxr-xr-x 4 root root`.

steps.title: Exercise: fix the access
steps.text:
A web application runs as the user `webapp`. Its files are under `/srv/webapp`. Three engineers in the group `devs` deploy it. You see this.


The application reports that it cannot save uploaded files, and `start.sh` fails with "Permission denied" when run. `database.conf` contains the database password.

List what is wrong with each of the five lines. Then write the commands to set sensible ownership and modes.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Problems**

1. `/srv/webapp` is `777`: any user or service can create and delete entries in it.
2. `database.conf` is `777`: every account on the machine can read the database password, and can replace the file.
3. `uploads` is owned by root with `755`. The application, running as `webapp`, is in "others" and cannot create files. This is the upload failure.
4. `start.sh` has no execute bit, which is the "Permission denied". It also belongs to one person, so the other engineers cannot update it.
5. `app.log` is writable by everyone, so any account can alter or erase the log.

**Commands**


**Notes**

- Not one of the fixes is `777`. Each grants a named user or group the least that works.
- Whether `devs` should be able to read `database.conf` is a decision. If engineers do not need the production password, make it `600`.
- A tighter design would make the code read-only for the `webapp` user and writable only by the deploy process, with `uploads` and `logs` as the only places the running application can write. An application that cannot change its own code is harder to take over.

choices.text: Only `deploy`
choices.feedback: The group set, `r-x`, also includes execute.

choices.text: `deploy` and `ana`
choices.feedback: The owner has `rwx`. Members of `ops` have `r-x`, which includes execute. Others have `---`, so `bilal` cannot even read it.

choices.text: Everyone
choices.feedback: The last three characters are `---`. Others have no access.

questions.prompt: What is the cause, and the right fix?

choices.feedback: The script ran. It failed when it tried to write.

choices.text: The directory is owned by root and only its owner may write. Give the directory to `deploy` with `chown`
choices.feedback: `deploy` falls in "others", which has `r-x`: it may list and enter, and may not create files. Changing the owner grants exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Permissions are too strict. Run `chmod 777` on it
choices.feedback: That would work, and it would let every user and service on the machine write there.

lessons.title: Processes and signals
lessons.intro: A running program is a process. This module covers how to see what is running, how to stop it properly, and how to keep something running after you log out.

steps.title: What a process is
steps.text:
A **process** is one running instance of a program. Starting the same program twice gives two processes.

Each process has:

- a **process ID** (PID), a number that identifies it while it lives,
- a **parent**, the process that started it,
- an **owner**, the user it runs as, which decides what it may touch,
- its own memory, open files and environment.

Processes form a tree. When the system boots, the first process starts (PID 1, usually `systemd`), and everything else descends from it. Your shell is a process, and each command you run is a child of it.

steps.title: Seeing what is running
steps.text:
`ps` lists processes. On its own it shows only those of your current terminal. Two forms show everything.



Read `USER` to see whose rights the process has, `%CPU` and `%MEM` for what it is using, and `RSS` for the memory it actually holds, in kilobytes. `TTY` is the terminal the process is attached to. A `?` there means none, which is normal for a service.

steps.title: Watching live
steps.text:
`top` shows the same information, refreshed every few seconds, sorted by processor use. `htop` is a friendlier version, where installed.


In `top`, press `M` to sort by memory and `P` to sort by processor. The top lines summarise the whole machine: load, memory in use and the number of processes. A later module explains those figures.

steps.title: Signals
steps.text:
You do not stop a process by reaching in and removing it. You send it a **signal**: a small numbered message from the system. The process can react to most signals in its own way.

| Signal | Number | Meaning | Can the process handle it? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SIGTERM` | 15 | Please finish and exit | Yes |
| `SIGINT` | 2 | Interrupt. Sent by Ctrl+C | Yes |
| `SIGHUP` | 1 | The terminal closed. Many services reload their configuration | Yes |
| `SIGKILL` | 9 | Stop now | No |
| `SIGSTOP` | 19 | Pause | No |
| `SIGCONT` | 18 | Resume after a pause | Yes |

`kill` sends a signal. Despite its name, its default is the polite one, `SIGTERM`.

steps.title: Ask first, force last
steps.text:
`SIGTERM` gives a program the chance to stop properly: finish the request it is handling, write its data, close its files, remove its lock file.

`SIGKILL` gives it nothing. The kernel removes the process at once. Whatever it was doing is cut off in the middle. A database killed this way has to recover when it next starts. A program writing a file leaves it half written. A lock file stays behind and may stop the next start.

So the order is always the same.

1. Send `SIGTERM`.
2. Wait a few seconds.
3. Only if it is still running, send `SIGKILL`.

Reaching for `kill -9` first is a habit worth unlearning. Container platforms and service managers follow the same order: a stop request sends `SIGTERM`, waits for a set time and then sends `SIGKILL`.

steps.title: Which signal
steps.text: A database process is slow to respond. An engineer wants to restart it and runs `kill -9` on its PID straight away.

steps.title: Foreground and background
steps.text:
A command you start normally runs in the **foreground**. The shell waits for it, and your keyboard is connected to it.

Adding `&` starts it in the **background**. The shell gives the prompt back at once.


A background job still writes to your terminal, which makes a mess, so its output is usually redirected to a file.

steps.title: Surviving a logout
steps.text:
A background job belongs to your shell. When you log out, or an SSH connection drops, the shell sends its jobs `SIGHUP`, and they stop. A long task started over SSH therefore dies with the connection.

There are three ways to prevent that, from simplest to best.


- `nohup` makes the command ignore the hangup. It is good enough for a single task.
- `tmux` (or `screen`) keeps a whole terminal session alive on the server. You can disconnect and return to it. It is the right tool for long interactive work.
- For anything that should always be running, such as an application, neither is right. That is a **service**, managed by the system, which starts it at boot and restarts it when it fails. A later module covers services.

steps.title: Exit status and zombies
steps.text:
When a process ends, it returns its exit status to its parent, as the first module described. The parent is expected to collect it.

A process that has ended and whose parent has not yet collected its status is a **zombie**. It appears in `ps` with the state `Z`. It uses no memory or processor, only a slot in the process table. A few zombies are harmless. Many of them point to a bug in the parent program. A zombie cannot be killed, since it is already dead. It goes away when its parent collects it or itself ends.

If a parent ends first, its children are adopted by PID 1, which collects them.

steps.title: What is using the file or the port
steps.text:
Two questions come up constantly.


`/proc` is a directory of information about running processes, one subdirectory per PID. It is not on disk. The kernel produces it on request.

A related surprise: deleting a file that a process still has open does not free the disk space. The name is gone and the data stays until the process closes the file. This is why deleting a huge log sometimes frees nothing, until the service that writes it is restarted.

steps.title: Priority
steps.text:
Every process has a **nice value** from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). A higher number is "nicer" to other processes. It matters only when the processor is contended.


Use it for batch work that should not disturb a live service.

steps.title: Closed laptop
steps.text: An engineer connects to a server over SSH and starts a 3-hour data import with `./import.sh &`. After 20 minutes they close their laptop and go home.

steps.title: Exercise: manage the processes
steps.text:
You are on a server and need to do each of these. Write the commands.

1. Find the PID and the owner of the process listening on port 8080.
2. See which five processes use the most memory.
3. A worker process with PID 7741 is stuck. Stop it properly, and only force it if needed.
4. Ask the `nginx` master process to reload its configuration without stopping. Its PID is in `/run/nginx.pid`.
5. Start `./reindex.sh`, which takes 4 hours, so that it survives your logout, and save its output.
6. You deleted a 40 GB log file and `df` shows no space was freed. Say why, and find the process responsible.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Notes**

- In task 2, `head -n 6` gives the header line plus five processes.
- In task 3, `ps -p 7741` succeeds only if the process still exists, so the `&&` sends `SIGKILL` only when `SIGTERM` did not work.
- In task 4, `SIGHUP` asks nginx to read its configuration again while it keeps serving. In practice `systemctl reload nginx` does the same and is the normal way.
- In task 5, a `tmux` session is the better choice if you want to return and watch it.
- In task 6, a process still has the deleted file open, so its data remains on disk. `lsof +L1` lists open files that no longer have a name. Restarting that process, or asking it to reopen its log, releases the space.

choices.text: None. `kill -9` is the standard way to stop a process
choices.feedback: It is the last resort. The standard way is `SIGTERM`.

choices.text: The database gets no chance to finish its writes and close cleanly, and must recover at the next start
choices.feedback: `SIGKILL` cannot be handled. Work in progress is cut off. A database is built to survive that, and recovery takes time and is a risk that `SIGTERM` would have avoided.

choices.text: The signal is ignored, since databases block signal 9
choices.feedback: No process can block or ignore `SIGKILL`.

choices.text: It keeps running, since `&` put it in the background
choices.feedback: Background means the shell does not wait for it. The job still belongs to that shell.

choices.text: It is stopped when the connection drops, since the shell sends its jobs a hangup signal
choices.feedback: The session ends, the shell exits, and its jobs receive `SIGHUP`. Use `tmux`, or `nohup` with output redirected.

choices.text: It pauses, and resumes when they reconnect
choices.feedback: Nothing pauses it and nothing would resume it. A new connection is a new shell.

lessons.title: Variables and the environment
lessons.intro: A shell remembers values in variables, and passes some of them to the programs it starts. This module covers how variables work, how the shell finds programs, how quoting changes what a command receives, and where settings are stored.

steps.title: Shell variables
steps.text:
A **variable** is a named value. Set one with `name=value`, with no spaces around the equals sign. Read it by putting `$` in front of the name.


The spaces matter. `name = "Ana"` runs a program called `name` with two arguments, and fails with "command not found".

Braces are needed when the name is followed directly by other characters. `$name_backup` is read as a variable called `name_backup`, which does not exist.

A variable that was never set is empty, and using it is not an error by default. That is a common source of bugs, and of the dangerous `rm -rf "$DIR/"` with an empty `DIR`.

steps.title: The environment
steps.text:
A plain variable belongs to the shell where it was set. Programs started from that shell do not see it.

`export` marks a variable as part of the **environment**: the set of variables that is copied to every program the shell starts. This is how configuration reaches a program.


The copy goes one way. A child process gets its own copy and can change it. The change never travels back to the parent. A script cannot change the variables of the shell that ran it.

steps.title: Variables you will meet
steps.text:
Some variables are set by the system and read by many programs.

| Variable | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `HOME` | Your home directory |
| `USER` | Your user name |
| `PATH` | The directories searched for programs |
| `PWD` | The current directory |
| `SHELL` | Your login shell |
| `LANG` | Language and character settings |
| `EDITOR` | The editor that programs open for you |

By convention, environment variables are written in capitals.

steps.title: How the shell finds a program
steps.text:
When you type `ls`, the shell has to find a file to run. It looks in each directory listed in `PATH`, in order, and runs the first match.


`PATH` is a list of directories separated by colons. Two things follow from the search order.

- **"command not found"** means no directory in `PATH` contains a program of that name. The program may be installed somewhere that is not on the list.
- **The first match wins.** If two versions are installed, the one in the earlier directory runs. `type -a` shows all of them.

The current directory is not in `PATH`. To run a program in the directory you are in, give a path: `./deploy.sh`. This is a safety feature, so that a file named `ls` placed in a shared directory is not run by accident.

Add a directory by putting it in front of the existing value.

steps.title: The wrong version
steps.text: A developer installs a new version of a tool into `/opt/tool/bin` and adds the line `export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tool/bin"` to their settings. An older version exists in `/usr/bin`. They run the tool.

steps.title: Quoting
steps.text:
Before running a command, the shell rewrites the line: it replaces variables, expands wildcards and splits the result into words. Quotes control how much of that happens.

| Form | Variables expanded? | Wildcards and word splitting? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No quotes | Yes | Yes |
| `"double quotes"` | Yes | No |
| `'single quotes'` | No | No |


The rule that prevents most shell bugs: **put double quotes around every variable**. Write `"$file"`, never bare `$file`. An unquoted variable that contains a space becomes several arguments, and one that contains `*` is expanded into file names.

Use single quotes when the text must reach the program exactly as written, as with `grep`, `sed` and `awk` patterns.

A backslash removes the special meaning of the one character after it: `\$` is a dollar sign and `\ ` is a space.

steps.title: Command substitution
steps.text:
`$(command)` runs a command and puts its output in its place.


Quote it for the same reason as a variable: `"$(command)"`.

steps.title: Where settings live
steps.text:
Variables and other settings last only for the session. To keep them, put them in a file the shell reads when it starts. These files are called **dotfiles**, since their names start with a dot.

| File | Read when |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.bashrc` | An interactive Bash shell starts, such as a new terminal window |
| `~/.profile` or `~/.bash_profile` | You log in, including over SSH |
| `/etc/profile`, `/etc/environment` | For every user on the system |

A common arrangement is for the login file to load `~/.bashrc`, so that both kinds of shell get the same settings.

A changed file takes effect in new shells. To apply it to the current one, **source** it.


`source file` runs the commands of a file in the current shell. That is the only way a file can change your current shell's variables. Running a script normally starts a child process, whose changes are lost when it ends.

steps.title: Aliases
steps.text:
An **alias** is a short name for a longer command. It lives in the same files.


Aliases are a personal convenience. They exist only in your interactive shell, so do not rely on them in scripts, and remember that another person's machine does not have yours.

steps.title: Configuration for applications
steps.text:
Environment variables are the standard way to give an application its settings, especially in containers and deployment pipelines. The same program then runs unchanged in test and production, and only its environment differs.

Two cautions.

- **A service does not read your dotfiles.** Something started by the system, a scheduler or a container has only the environment it was given. "It works in my terminal and not as a service" very often means a variable that exists only in your shell.
- **The environment is not private.** Root and the process's owner can read a running process's environment, and it is easy to print in a log. Secrets need more care than a line in `.bashrc`.

steps.title: Works in the terminal
steps.text: A script runs correctly when an engineer starts it by hand. Run from a scheduled job at night, it fails with `pg_dump: command not found`. The engineer's `~/.bashrc` contains `export PATH="/usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin:$PATH"`.

steps.title: Exercise: explain and fix
steps.text:
For each situation, say what is happening and what to change.

1. `backup_dir = /srv/backups` gives `backup_dir: command not found`.
2. A script contains `rm -rf $TARGET/*`. The variable `TARGET` was meant to be set by an earlier step that failed.
3. `echo "Total: $count_items"` prints `Total:` although `count` is set to 12. The intent was to print `12_items`.
4. A user runs a script that contains `export API_URL=https://staging.example.com`, and afterwards `echo $API_URL` in their terminal prints nothing.
5. `for f in $(ls *.txt)` breaks on a file named `annual report.txt`.
6. `grep $pattern file.txt` behaves oddly when `pattern` is `a*`.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Spaces around `=`.** The shell reads `backup_dir` as a program name. Write `backup_dir=/srv/backups`.
2. **An empty variable.** With `TARGET` unset, the line becomes `rm -rf /*`, which tries to delete the whole system. Quote it and refuse to run when it is empty: `rm -rf "${TARGET:?}"/*`. The `:?` makes the shell stop with an error if the variable is unset or empty. The scripts module adds `set -u`, which catches every such case.
3. **The name runs on.** The shell looks for a variable called `count_items`. Use braces: `"Total: ${count}_items"`.
4. **A child process.** The script ran in its own process, and its `export` ended with it. To change the current shell, run it with `source script.sh`.
5. **Word splitting.** The output of `ls` is split on spaces, so the name becomes two words. Do not parse `ls`. Let the shell match the files: `for f in *.txt`, and use `"$f"` inside the loop.
6. **An unquoted variable.** The shell expands `a*` against the file names in the directory before `grep` runs. If files match, `grep` receives those names in place of the pattern. Write `grep "$pattern" file.txt`.

Four of the six come from one cause: text was expanded or split when it should have been passed through whole. Quoting variables removes most of this class of problem.

lessons.title: Shell scripts
lessons.intro: A shell script is a file of commands that the shell runs in order. It turns a procedure you would type by hand into something repeatable. This module covers how to write one, how to make it stop when something goes wrong, and when a script is the wrong tool.

steps.title: A first script
steps.text:
A script is a text file. Three things make it runnable.



The first line, starting with `#!`, is the **shebang**. It tells the system which program should read the file. `#!/usr/bin/env bash` means "find bash on the `PATH` and use it".

Without a shebang, the file is run by whatever shell happens to be in use, and that differs between systems. On many, `/bin/sh` is not Bash and lacks some of its features. State which shell you wrote the script for.

Lines starting with `#` are comments.

steps.title: Make the script stop on errors
steps.text:
By default, a script continues after a command fails. It runs the next line as if nothing had happened. This is the most dangerous property of shell scripts.

Put this line at the top of every Bash script.


| Setting | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-e` | Stop as soon as a command fails |
| `-u` | Treat the use of an unset variable as an error |
| `-o pipefail` | A pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not only the last |

Each one removes a way for a script to do harm quietly. `-u` alone prevents the empty-variable `rm -rf` from the previous module.

`-e` has exceptions. A command whose failure is tested, as in an `if` or before `||`, does not stop the script. Where a failure is expected and acceptable, say so explicitly: `rm tmpfile || true`.

steps.title: The script that kept going
steps.text: A deploy script has no `set -e`. Its steps are: build the application, run the tests, copy the build to the server, restart the service. The tests fail.

steps.title: Arguments
steps.text:
Values given after a script's name are available inside it as numbered variables.

| Variable | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `$1`, `$2`, ... | The first argument, the second, and so on |
| `$0` | The name of the script |
| `$#` | How many arguments were given |
| `"$@"` | All the arguments, each kept as one word |


Check the arguments first, print a usage message to standard error if they are wrong, and exit with a non-zero status. A script that carries on with a missing argument does something unintended.

`"$@"`, in quotes, is the correct way to pass all arguments on to another command.

steps.title: Tests and conditions
steps.text:
`if` runs a command and looks at its exit status. Zero means true.


The square brackets are a command that tests a condition. `[[ ... ]]` is Bash's improved form, which is more forgiving about quoting. Spaces are required inside the brackets.

| Test | True when |
| --- | --- |
| `[ -f path ]` | A file exists |
| `[ -d path ]` | A directory exists |
| `[ -s path ]` | A file exists and is not empty |
| `[ -z "$var" ]` | The value is empty |
| `[ -n "$var" ]` | The value is not empty |
| `[ "$a" = "$b" ]` | Two strings are equal |
| `[ "$a" -eq "$b" ]` | Two numbers are equal (`-ne`, `-lt`, `-gt`, `-le`, `-ge`) |

Text and numbers use different operators. `=` compares strings, and `-eq` compares numbers.

steps.title: Loops
steps.text: Quote the loop variable where you use it, as in `"$f"`, so that names with spaces survive.

steps.title: Functions
steps.text:
A **function** names a group of commands, so that a script reads as a list of steps.


Inside a function, `$1` and `$2` are the function's own arguments. Declare variables with `local`, or they are visible to the whole script and can overwrite each other.

A function returns an exit status, with `return`, and sends data back by printing it.

steps.title: Exit status and cleanup
steps.text:
A script should end with a status that says whether it worked. Other scripts, schedulers and pipelines rely on it.


`trap ... EXIT` registers a command to run when the script ends, for any reason, including an error. It is the reliable way to remove temporary files or release a lock.

`mktemp` creates a temporary file or directory with a unique, unpredictable name. Use it in place of a fixed name such as `/tmp/work`, which two runs of the script would fight over.

steps.title: Habits that prevent damage
steps.text:
- **Quote every variable**: `"$var"`.
- **Start with `set -euo pipefail`.**
- **Check arguments and required tools** at the top.
- **Send error messages to standard error**, with `>&2`.
- **Use full paths** for files, and do not depend on the directory the script was started from.
- **Offer a dry run** for anything destructive: a mode that prints what would be done.
- **Make it safe to run twice.** `mkdir -p` and "create if missing" steps let a script be run again after a partial failure.
- **Run a linter.** `shellcheck` reads a script and reports quoting mistakes and other common faults.

steps.title: Scheduling
steps.text:
To run a script regularly, give it to a scheduler. The traditional one is **cron**. Each user has a table of jobs, edited with `crontab -e`.


Scheduled jobs fail in their own ways.

- They run with a minimal environment. Your `PATH` and variables are not there. Use full paths.
- Nobody is watching. Redirect output to a log, and make failures visible.
- A long job may still be running when the next run starts. Use a lock so that two copies do not overlap.

On current systems, systemd timers do the same job with better logging. The services module mentions them.

steps.title: When not to write a shell script
steps.text:
Shell is the right tool for gluing commands together: run these five programs in order and stop if one fails.

It is the wrong tool when the script needs real data structures, arithmetic beyond counting, careful error handling, JSON, or tests. Shell has many traps, and they multiply with length.

A reasonable rule is that when a script passes about a hundred lines, or starts to need arrays and string handling, it should be rewritten in a general programming language.

steps.title: Tested or not
steps.text: A script starts with `set -e`. One line is `grep -q "ready" status.txt`, used as a plain statement to check that a service is ready. The word is not in the file.

steps.title: Exercise: review the script
steps.text: This script is meant to archive yesterday's logs and delete the originals. List every problem you can find. Then rewrite it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Problems**

1. **No shebang.** It may be run by a shell other than the one intended.
2. **No `set -e`.** If `cd` fails, `tar` and `rm` run in whatever directory the script was started from, and `rm *.log` deletes the wrong files.
3. **Deleting after a possible failure.** If `tar` fails, for example on a full disk, `rm` still runs. The logs are gone and no archive exists.
4. **A fixed archive name.** Each run overwrites the previous archive. Only one day is ever kept.
5. **No check that anything matched.** With no `.log` files, the pattern stays as the literal text `*.log` and both commands fail in a confusing way.
6. **Files in use.** The application may still be writing to the current log. Deleting it loses lines and may not free the space.
7. **No useful exit status or messages.** It prints "done" whatever happened.

**Rewritten**


**What changed**

- `set -euo pipefail` means a failed `cd` or `tar` ends the script before anything is deleted.
- The archive name includes the date, so earlier days are kept.
- It takes only yesterday's rotated logs, by name, and leaves the file the application is writing.
- `nullglob` makes a pattern with no matches expand to nothing, and the empty case is handled as a normal outcome.
- The archive is read back before the originals are removed.

It is now about twenty lines, with an array in it. That is close to the point where another language would be the better choice.

choices.feedback: Nothing told it to. A failed command only sets an exit status.

choices.text: It prints the test failures, then copies the build and restarts the service anyway
choices.feedback: Without `set -e` every line runs regardless. A build that failed its tests is now live.

choices.text: It skips the copy and still restarts the service
choices.feedback: The shell has no notion of which later steps depend on which earlier ones.

choices.text: The script stops at that line
choices.feedback: `grep` exits with status 1 when nothing matches, and with `set -e` a failing command ends the script. If "not found" is an expected outcome, test it with `if`.

choices.text: The script continues, since `grep` printed no error
choices.feedback: A missing match prints nothing and still returns a non-zero status.

choices.text: The script continues, since `-q` hides the failure
choices.feedback: `-q` hides the output. The exit status is unchanged.

lessons.title: Install and update software
lessons.intro: Software on Linux is installed from packages that a package manager fetches, checks and tracks. This module covers how that works, how to keep a system updated, and how to work out what is installed and where it came from.

steps.title: Distributions and package managers
steps.text:
Linux itself is a kernel. A **distribution** combines it with tools, libraries and a way to install software. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Alpine are distributions.

Each family has its own **package manager** and package format.

| Family | Examples | Package manager | Format |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Debian | Debian, Ubuntu | `apt` | `.deb` |
| Red Hat | Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Amazon Linux | `dnf` (older: `yum`) | `.rpm` |
| Alpine | Alpine, common in containers | `apk` | `.apk` |

The commands differ and the ideas are the same. This module shows `apt`, with the others beside it where it helps.

Find out what you are on before anything else.

steps.title: Packages and repositories
steps.text:
A **package** is an archive holding a program's files together with a description: its name, version, what it depends on, and scripts to run at install and removal.

A **repository** is a server that holds thousands of packages with an index of them. The package manager is configured with a list of repositories. It downloads their indexes, and from those it knows what is available.

A package manager does four things that a manual download does not.

- **Resolves dependencies.** If a program needs three libraries, they are installed with it.
- **Verifies.** Packages and indexes are signed, and the signature is checked, so a tampered package is refused.
- **Tracks.** It records every file each package installed, so the package can be removed cleanly or checked later.
- **Updates.** It can upgrade everything installed in one step.

steps.title: The everyday commands
steps.text:
`apt update` does not update any software. It refreshes the list of available versions. `apt upgrade` is what installs newer versions. Running `install` or `upgrade` against a stale index is a common cause of "package not found" and "404" errors, especially in a container image built long ago.

| Task | Debian family | Red Hat family | Alpine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Refresh the index | `apt update` | (done automatically) | `apk update` |
| Install | `apt install x` | `dnf install x` | `apk add x` |
| Remove | `apt remove x` | `dnf remove x` | `apk del x` |
| Upgrade all | `apt upgrade` | `dnf upgrade` | `apk upgrade` |
| Search | `apt search x` | `dnf search x` | `apk search x` |

steps.title: Package not found
steps.text: In a fresh container based on a Debian image, the first command a user runs is `apt install curl`. It fails with "Unable to locate package curl".

steps.title: What is installed, and from where
steps.text:
The last two answer a different question from the first four. `which` and `-v` tell you about the program that runs when you type the name. That may not be the packaged one, if a second copy was installed by hand and comes earlier in `PATH`.

When a program behaves unexpectedly, check both: which file runs, and which package, if any, owns that file.

steps.title: Keeping a system updated
steps.text:
Updates fix security flaws. A server that is never updated collects known, published vulnerabilities.

- **Security updates** should be applied promptly. Most distributions can install them automatically. On Debian and Ubuntu this is the `unattended-upgrades` package.
- **Some updates need a restart to take effect.** A new kernel runs only after a reboot. A service keeps using an old library until it is restarted. Ubuntu creates the file `/var/run/reboot-required` when a reboot is pending.
- **Distribution releases have an end of life.** After that date, no more security fixes arrive. Know the date for what you run, and plan the move to a newer release before it.

steps.title: Versions and holding them
steps.text:
A distribution release ships one version of each package and, as a rule, keeps to it. Fixes are applied to that version, and it does not jump to a new major version. That stability is the point: an update should not break what works.

It also means the packaged version of a tool may be old. There are several ways to get a newer one, each with a cost.

- **The vendor's own repository.** Many projects publish one. You add it and its signing key, and the package manager handles the rest. This is the best option where it exists.
- **A version manager** for a language runtime, which installs versions under your home directory.
- **A container**, which carries its own version and leaves the host alone.
- **Building from source,** which nothing tracks and nothing updates.

To stop a package from being upgraded, hold it.


A held package also misses security fixes, so hold with a reason and review the list.

steps.title: Adding a repository is a matter of trust
steps.text:
A repository can install anything on your system as root. Its packages run install scripts with full rights. Adding one is the same decision as giving its owner administrator access.

- Add only repositories from sources you have reason to trust.
- Use the repository's signing key, so that packages are verified.
- Prefer the distribution's own packages where they are good enough.

The same caution applies to the common instruction "run this to install", which pipes a script from a web address straight into a shell.


Reading an install script takes a few minutes, and it shows what it will change on your system. This is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

steps.title: Other ways software arrives
steps.text:
Not everything comes from the system package manager.

| Source | Example | Tracked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System packages | `apt install nginx` | The package manager |
| Language package managers | `pip`, `npm`, `gem`, `cargo` | That tool, per project or per user |
| Universal packages | `snap`, `flatpak` | Their own tools |
| A downloaded binary | A file copied to `/usr/local/bin` | Nothing |
| Source code | `make install` | Nothing |
| Containers | An image | The container runtime |

Problems begin when these overlap. Installing a library with the system package manager and again with a language's own tool gives two copies, and which one a program picks up depends on search order. Keep them apart: system packages for the system, and a project's own dependencies inside the project or in a container.

By convention, software installed by hand goes under `/usr/local` or `/opt`, so that it never collides with files the package manager owns.

steps.title: Two of the same
steps.text: A server has a tool installed from the distribution's package at `/usr/bin/tool`, version 2.1. Later someone installs version 3.0 by hand into `/usr/local/bin/tool`. `PATH` is `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`. A month later, `apt upgrade` updates the package to version 2.2.

steps.title: Exercise: work out what is going on
steps.text:
You are asked to look at a server. Write the commands you would run for each question, and say what you would conclude.

1. Which distribution and release is this, and is it still supported?
2. Is `openssl` installed, at what version, and from which repository?
3. A colleague says `node --version` prints `v14.21.3`, although they "installed version 20 last week". How do you find out why?
4. Are security updates outstanding, and is a reboot pending?
5. Someone wants to install a tool by running `curl ... | sudo bash` from a blog post. What do you suggest?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Conclusions**

1. The file gives the name and version. Compare the version with the distribution's published end-of-life date. If that date has passed, upgrading the release is the first job, since nothing else will receive fixes.
2. `dpkg -l` shows whether it is installed and its version. `apt-cache policy` shows which repository that version came from and whether a newer one is available.
3. `type -a` lists every `node` on the `PATH`, in search order. Almost certainly there are two: the old one in an earlier directory, and version 20 somewhere later, or in a directory that is not on the `PATH` at all for this user or service. `dpkg -S` shows whether the file that runs belongs to a package. The fix is to remove the old one or to put the right directory first.
4. The list shows what would be upgraded. If the reboot file exists, an earlier update is waiting for a restart, and the machine is still running the old kernel or libraries.
5. Download the script and read it first. Look for an official package or the vendor's repository, which would also deliver updates. If the script is the only way, run it in a test machine or a container before a server, and avoid `sudo` unless the script truly needs it. This is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

choices.text: Neither. The package manager removes the conflicting copy
