lessons.title: Services and logs
lessons.intro: A server's real work is done by programs that run all the time without anyone logged in. This module covers how those services are started, stopped and kept alive, and where to read what they say when something goes wrong.

steps.title: What a service is
steps.text:
A **service** (also called a daemon) is a program that runs in the background for as long as the machine is up: a web server, a database, the SSH server.

A service needs things that a program started from a terminal does not get.

- It starts when the machine boots, with nobody logged in.
- It is restarted if it crashes.
- It runs as its own user, with limited rights.
- Its output is collected somewhere.
- It starts after the things it needs, such as the network.

A **service manager** provides these. On almost every current distribution it is **systemd**, which is also the first process, PID 1. You talk to it with the command `systemctl`.

steps.title: Controlling a service
steps.text:
Two pairs are easy to confuse.

**Start and enable are separate.** `start` runs the service now. `enable` arranges for it to start at boot. A service that was started and not enabled is gone after the next reboot. A service that was enabled and not started is not running yet.

**Restart and reload are separate.** `restart` stops the process and starts a new one, which drops the connections in progress. `reload` asks the running process to read its configuration again without stopping. Use `reload` where the service supports it.

steps.title: Reading the status
steps.text:
`systemctl status` is the first command to run when a service misbehaves. It shows the state and the last few log lines together.


Read three things.

- **Loaded:** where the definition file is, and whether the service is `enabled` for boot.
- **Active:** the state now, and since when. `active (running)` is healthy. `failed` means it exited with an error. `activating (auto-restart)` that keeps recurring means it is crashing and being restarted in a loop.
- **The log lines at the bottom**, which usually say why.

A service that started seconds ago, when you expected it to have been up for days, has been restarting.

steps.title: Unit files
steps.text:
systemd describes each thing it manages in a **unit file**. A service's unit file says what to run and how.


| Line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `After=` | Start this after the named unit |
| `User=` | Run as this user, not as root |
| `EnvironmentFile=` | Read environment variables from this file |
| `ExecStart=` | The command to run. Give the program's full path |
| `Restart=on-failure` | Start it again if it exits with an error |
| `WantedBy=multi-user.target` | What `enable` attaches it to: normal boot |

Unit files supplied by packages live in `/lib/systemd/system`. Your own, and your changes, go in `/etc/systemd/system`, which takes priority. After changing any unit file, tell systemd to read them again.


`systemctl edit` creates a small override file and leaves the packaged file alone, so that a package update does not undo your change.

steps.title: Gone after the reboot
steps.text: An engineer installs a new service, writes its unit file, runs `sudo systemctl start orders`, checks that it works and goes home. That night the server is rebooted for a kernel update.

steps.title: Why a service differs from your terminal
steps.text:
"It works when I run it by hand and fails as a service" is a common report. A service runs in a different setting.

| | In your terminal | As a service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User | You | The `User=` in the unit, often with fewer rights |
| Environment | Your dotfiles, your `PATH` | Only what the unit sets |
| Working directory | Where you happen to be | `WorkingDirectory=`, or `/` |
| Input | Your keyboard | None |
| Output | The screen | The journal |

So check, in order: can that user read the files and write where it needs to? Does the program rely on a variable or a `PATH` entry from your shell? Does it use a relative path that assumes a directory?

steps.title: The journal
steps.text:
systemd collects the output of every service, along with system messages, in the **journal**. `journalctl` reads it.


Whatever a service prints to standard output or standard error lands here, with a timestamp and the service's name. A program does not need to manage a log file of its own. It can simply print.

`-u` selects a unit, and nearly every investigation starts with it. Add `--since` to narrow the time, since a busy service produces a great deal.

steps.title: Log files
steps.text:
Not everything uses the journal. Many programs write their own files, by convention under `/var/log`.

| File or directory | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/messages` | General system messages |
| `/var/log/auth.log` or `/var/log/secure` | Logins, `sudo` use, SSH attempts |
| `/var/log/nginx/` | The web server's access and error logs |
| `/var/log/apt/` or `/var/log/dnf.log` | What was installed and when |
| `/var/log/kern.log` | Kernel messages |

The names differ between distribution families. `ls -lt /var/log | head` shows which files changed most recently, which is a quick way to find the one that matters.

steps.title: Rotation
steps.text:
A log that grows for ever fills the disk. **Log rotation** prevents it. On a schedule, the current file is renamed, a new empty one is started, old ones are compressed, and the oldest are deleted.


The tool is `logrotate`, configured by files in `/etc/logrotate.d`. The journal limits its own size separately.

Two consequences come up in practice. Searching for something from last week means searching the rotated files too, with `zgrep` for the compressed ones. And an application that writes its own log file with no rotation rule is a full disk waiting to happen.

steps.title: When a service will not start
steps.text:
Work through the same steps each time.

1. `systemctl status <name>`. Read the state and the last lines.
2. `journalctl -u <name> -n 100`. Read upward from the end to the first error.
3. Run the `ExecStart` command by hand as the service's user: `sudo -u orders /srv/orders/bin/server --port 8080`. The error then prints straight to your terminal.
4. Check what it needs: the configuration file, the port, the permissions, the dependency it connects to.

The message is nearly always there. The usual ones are:

| Message | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `Address already in use` | Another process holds the port |
| `Permission denied` | The service's user cannot read or write something |
| `No such file or directory` | A wrong path, often a relative one |
| `status=203/EXEC` | systemd could not run the program: wrong path, or not executable |
| `Start request repeated too quickly` | It crashed repeatedly, and systemd gave up |

For the last one, the cause is in the earlier lines. After fixing it, `sudo systemctl reset-failed <name>` clears the state.

steps.title: Timers
steps.text: systemd can also run something on a schedule, as cron does. A **timer** unit starts a service unit at set times. Its advantages over cron are that the output goes to the journal like any other service, and that a run missed while the machine was off can be caught up.

steps.title: The crash loop
steps.text: `systemctl status orders` shows `Active: activating (auto-restart)`, and the start time changes every few seconds. The last journal line reads `Error: cannot open /etc/orders/env: Permission denied`.

steps.title: Exercise: bring the service up
steps.text:
A colleague wrote this unit file for a small API and reports that it "does not work". The API listens on port 80 and reads `config.yaml` from its own directory.


They ran `sudo systemctl start reports`, and `systemctl status reports` shows `failed` with `status=203/EXEC`. They also mention that, when it did run once in their terminal, it ran as root.

List the problems with the unit file. Write a corrected one, and the commands to put it into effect and check it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Problems**

1. **`ExecStart` has no full path.** systemd does not use your shell's `PATH`, and the program is not in the few system directories it does search. This is the `203/EXEC` error.
2. **A relative path to the configuration,** with no working directory set. A service starts in `/`, so `config.yaml` is not found.
3. **No user.** It runs as root, so a flaw in the API is a flaw with full control of the machine.
4. **Port 80 needs a privilege.** Ports below 1024 cannot be opened by an ordinary user. Listen on a high port behind a proxy, or grant only that one capability.
5. **No restart policy.** A crash leaves it down.
6. **No ordering.** It may start before the network is ready.

**Corrected**


**Put it into effect**


`AmbientCapabilities` lets the unprivileged user open port 80 and nothing else. `daemon-reload` is needed because the unit file changed. `enable --now` starts the service and makes it survive a reboot. The last two commands check the result, which is the step most often skipped.

choices.feedback: Starting a service and enabling it at boot are separate steps. `sudo systemctl enable --now orders` does both.

choices.text: The service exits at start because its user cannot read that file, and systemd keeps restarting it
choices.feedback: `Restart=on-failure` restarts it each time. Check the owner and mode of `/etc/orders/env` against the `User=` in the unit, and of the directory that holds it.

choices.text: systemd is broken and must be restarted
choices.feedback: systemd is doing what the unit asked. The program is the part that fails.

lessons.title: Network tools
lessons.intro: Sooner or later a server cannot reach something, or cannot be reached. This module covers the commands that show a machine's network setup and test each step of a connection. The Networking course explains the ideas behind them. This one is about the tools.

steps.title: The machine's own setup
steps.text:
Start by looking at what the machine has: its addresses, its routes and its name servers.



Read it like this. `lo` is the loopback interface, which every machine has. `eth0` has the address `10.0.1.5` in a `/24` subnet. `UP` means the interface is enabled. The `default via` line names the gateway used for everything outside the subnet.

No address on the interface, or no `default` line, explains a machine that can reach nothing. Older guides use `ifconfig` and `route` for the same information. The `ip` command replaced them.

steps.title: What is listening
steps.text:
A service that should accept connections has to be listening on a port. `ss` shows which ports are open and which process holds each.



Read the `Local Address:Port` column and the process at the end. On a real terminal each entry is one long line. It is wrapped here to fit.

The address in front of the port decides who can connect. `127.0.0.1:5432` accepts connections from this machine only. `0.0.0.0:80` accepts them on every interface. `[::]` is the same for IPv6.

The options are worth knowing: `-l` listening, `-t` TCP, `-u` UDP, `-n` numbers and not names, `-p` the process. `sudo` is needed to see processes that belong to other users. Older guides use `netstat` with similar options.

steps.title: Names
steps.text:
`dig` asks DNS a question and shows the full answer. `getent hosts` resolves a name the way programs on this machine do, which includes the local file `/etc/hosts`.


The difference between the last two and `dig` matters. `/etc/hosts` is checked before DNS. A stale line there makes one machine resolve a name differently from every other, and `dig` will not show it, since `dig` talks only to DNS. When a name behaves oddly on a single machine, read `/etc/hosts`.

steps.title: Can I reach it
steps.text:
Test reachability in steps, each a little higher than the one before.


`ping` sends a small test packet and reports whether a reply came, and how long it took. `-c 4` sends four and stops. On Linux, without it, `ping` runs until you press Ctrl+C.

The `-w 3` makes `nc` give up after 3 seconds. Without it, a blocked connection can hang for minutes.

A failed `ping` proves little, since many networks block those packets while allowing real traffic. A successful TCP connection with `nc -vz` proves much more: the path works and something is listening.

`nc` gives three different results, and each has a meaning.

| Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `succeeded` or `open` | The path and the port are fine |
| `Connection refused`, at once | The machine answered, and nothing listens on that port |
| `timed out`, after a wait | A firewall dropped it, or the address is unreachable |

steps.title: HTTP with curl
steps.text:
`curl` makes a request and prints the response. It is the main tool for testing anything that speaks HTTP.


`-v` is the one to remember. It shows the address the name resolved to, the connection, the TLS handshake and certificate, the request sent and the response received. Wherever the output stops is where the problem is.

The fifth line prints only the status code, which is useful in scripts. In a script, also add `--fail`, so that an HTTP error status gives a non-zero exit status, and `--max-time`, so that a hung server cannot hang the script.

steps.title: Refused or timed out
steps.text: From an application server, `nc -vz 10.0.2.8 5432` prints `Connection refused` immediately. On the database server `10.0.2.8`, `ss -ltnp` shows `LISTEN 127.0.0.1:5432`.

steps.title: The local firewall
steps.text:
A machine can filter its own traffic. Several tools manage the same underlying kernel feature, and which one is in use depends on the distribution.


When a service is listening on the right address and remote clients still time out, the local firewall is the next thing to check, followed by the firewall rules of the network or cloud platform outside the machine.

steps.title: Copying files between machines
steps.text:
Both run over SSH. `scp` copies everything each time. `rsync` compares the two sides and sends only the differences, so it is much faster for repeated copies and can resume after an interruption.

With `rsync`, a trailing slash on the source changes the meaning. `site/` copies the contents of the directory. `site` copies the directory itself, creating `site` inside the destination. `--delete` removes files at the destination that are not in the source, so run it with `-n` first and read what it would do.

steps.title: Downloading
steps.text:
`-f` makes `curl` fail on an HTTP error, so an error page is not saved as if it were the file. `-L` follows redirects and `-O` keeps the remote file name.

When a download page publishes a checksum, compute yours and compare. A match shows the file arrived complete and is the one that was published.

steps.title: A method for "it cannot connect"
steps.text:
Put the tools in the order a connection is made, and stop at the first step that fails.

1. **Is my own network up?** `ip addr`, `ip route`.
2. **Does the name resolve?** `dig +short name`, and `getent hosts name`.
3. **Is the port reachable?** `nc -vz address port`.
4. **Does the service answer correctly?** `curl -v`.
5. **On the server:** is it listening, and on which address? `ss -ltnp`. Is a local firewall in the way?

Run the same test from two places when you can. If it works from the server itself and fails from another machine, the fault is the listening address or a firewall. If it works by address and fails by name, the fault is DNS.

steps.title: One machine disagrees
steps.text: Every server resolves `db.internal.example.com` to `10.0.2.8`. One application server keeps connecting to `10.0.2.3`, an address that was retired last month. On that server, `dig +short db.internal.example.com` prints `10.0.2.8`.

steps.title: Exercise: find the fault
steps.text:
A new application server, `app03` at `10.0.1.30`, cannot reach the internal API at `https://api.internal.example.com`. The other application servers can. You run these on `app03`.


Say which steps are proven to work, what the fault is, how you would confirm it by comparing with a working server, and what the fix is. Then say what you would check next, once the fix is in.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Proven to work.** The interface is up and has an address. DNS resolves the name, so the name servers are reachable. A connection to `10.0.1.9`, a machine in the same subnet, succeeds.

**The fault.** "Network is unreachable" is the machine's own kernel speaking: it has no route for that destination. The route table shows why. It has the route for the local subnet and no `default via` line. The API is at `10.0.4.12`, in another subnet, and without a default gateway `app03` has nowhere to send the packet. Machines in `10.0.1.0/24` work, since they need no gateway.

That DNS works suggests the name server is in the local subnet as well.

**Confirm.** Run `ip route` on a working application server. It will have a line such as `default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0`.

**Fix.** Add the default route. For an immediate test: `sudo ip route add default via 10.0.1.1`. That lasts until reboot. The permanent fix belongs in the machine's network configuration, or in whatever built `app03`, since it was created without a gateway and the next server will be too.

**Next.** Move up the steps. Run `nc -vz 10.0.4.12 443` again. If it now times out, a firewall rule probably does not include the new server's address yet. Then `curl -v https://api.internal.example.com/health` to check TLS and the response.

The message decided the direction. "Unreachable" pointed at this machine's routes. "Refused" would have pointed at the API server, and a timeout at a firewall in between.

choices.text: A firewall between the two servers
choices.feedback: A firewall that drops packets causes a timeout. The refusal came back at once, so the database server itself answered.

choices.text: The database listens only on the loopback address, so connections from other machines are refused
choices.feedback: Nothing listens on port 5432 at the server's network address. The database's listen address needs to include that interface.

choices.text: The database is not running
choices.feedback: `ss` shows it listening. It is listening in the wrong place for this purpose.

choices.text: The database's own configuration
choices.feedback: The database does not decide what address clients look up.

lessons.title: Remote access with SSH
lessons.intro:
SSH is how you get a shell on a machine that is somewhere else. This module covers how it identifies the server and you, how to use keys in place of passwords, and how to make daily use of it short and safe.

The security advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: What SSH gives you
steps.text:
**SSH** (secure shell) opens an encrypted connection to another machine and runs a shell there. Everything you type and everything the machine answers is encrypted on the way.


The form is `ssh user@host`. Without `user@`, your local user name is used. With a command on the end, SSH runs that command on the remote machine and returns, without an interactive shell. That makes it usable in scripts.

Watch your prompt. It names the machine you are on. Running a command on the wrong machine is an easy and sometimes costly mistake.

steps.title: Knowing the server
steps.text:
The first time you connect to a machine, SSH shows a **host key fingerprint** and asks whether to continue.


Every server has its own key pair. The fingerprint identifies it. When you answer yes, the key is saved in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. On every later connection, SSH checks that the server presents the same key and says nothing if it does.

If the key has changed, SSH refuses to connect and prints a large warning. There are two possible reasons. The server was rebuilt or replaced, which is common and harmless. Or something is pretending to be the server, in order to capture what you send.

Do not delete the old entry by reflex. Find out why the key changed. If the server was rebuilt, remove the old key with `ssh-keygen -R hostname` and connect again.

Strictly, the fingerprint at first connection should be compared with one obtained through another channel, such as the cloud console. Few people do. It is the one moment at which SSH cannot protect you by itself.

steps.title: Passwords and keys
steps.text:
SSH can identify you by a password or by a **key pair**. Keys are better in every way that matters.

A key pair has two parts.

- The **private key** stays on your machine and is never shared or copied to a server.
- The **public key** is placed on each server you want to reach. It is safe to hand to anyone.

At login, the server sends a challenge, your client answers using the private key, and the server checks the answer against the public key. The private key never leaves your machine. A server that is compromised learns nothing it could use to log in elsewhere as you.

| | Password | Key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can be guessed | Yes, and automated guessing is constant | No, not in practice |
| Sent to the server | Yes | No |
| Reused across servers | The same secret everywhere | One public key, safe to place anywhere |
| Works in scripts | Poorly | Yes |

Servers that face the internet receive password guesses all day. Turning password login off, and allowing only keys, ends that whole class of attack.

steps.title: Creating and installing a key
steps.text:
`ed25519` is the current recommended key type. `ssh-copy-id` adds your public key to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server, which is the list of keys allowed to log in as that user.

Set a **passphrase** when asked. It encrypts the private key file. Without one, anyone who copies that file from your laptop or a backup can log in as you. With one, the file alone is useless.

SSH insists on strict permissions and silently ignores files that are too open.

steps.title: Which file goes where
steps.text: A new engineer needs access to a server. They create a key pair and send both files, `id_ed25519` and `id_ed25519.pub`, to the administrator by chat, "so it can be set up".

steps.title: The agent
steps.text:
Typing a passphrase at every connection is tedious, and the tedium tempts people to leave it empty. The **SSH agent** solves that. It is a small program that holds your unlocked keys in memory for the session.


After that, connections use the key without asking. Most desktop systems start an agent for you and tie it to your login.

**Agent forwarding** (`ssh -A`) lets a server you are logged in to use the agent on your laptop, so that you can connect onward from it. Be careful with it. While you are connected, anyone with root on that server can use your agent to log in elsewhere as you. Forward only to machines you fully trust. For reaching a machine through another, the jump host option below is safer.

steps.title: The config file
steps.text:
`~/.ssh/config` stores settings per host, so that long commands become short names.


With this file, `ssh web01` is enough. The settings also apply to `scp`, `rsync` and anything else that runs over SSH.

`ServerAliveInterval 60` sends a small message every minute, which stops idle connections from being cut by firewalls on the way.

steps.title: Jump hosts
steps.text:
Servers in a private network are often reachable only through one hardened machine, called a **bastion** or jump host. `ProxyJump` connects through it in one step.


Your connection to the inner machine is encrypted end to end, through the bastion. Your key is used from your laptop and is never placed on the bastion.

steps.title: Tunnels
steps.text:
SSH can also carry other connections inside its own. This is **port forwarding**.


The database accepts connections only from inside the private network. The tunnel lets a tool on your laptop reach it, through a server that can.

A tunnel lasts as long as the SSH session, and it bypasses whatever network rules would otherwise apply. Use it for short tasks, close it afterwards, and follow your organization's rules about reaching production data.

steps.title: Securing the server side
steps.text:
The SSH server's settings are in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`. A few lines matter most.


- **Keys only** ends password guessing.
- **No root login** means every session belongs to a named person, and their use of `sudo` is logged.
- **Limit who can reach port 22**, with a firewall, to a bastion or a VPN where possible.
- **Remove keys when people leave.** A line in `authorized_keys` works until someone deletes it.

Before reloading the SSH server after a change, keep your current session open and test a new login from a second terminal. A mistake in this file can lock everyone out, and an open session is your way back in.

steps.title: When it will not connect
steps.text:
`ssh -v` prints each step of the connection: resolving the name, connecting, checking the host key, offering each key, and the server's answer.

| Message | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `Connection timed out` | A firewall, a wrong address, or the machine is down |
| `Connection refused` | Nothing listens on that port |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | The server accepted none of your keys |
| `Host key verification failed` | The server's key differs from the saved one |
| `Too many authentication failures` | The agent offered several wrong keys first |
| `UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE` | The key file's permissions are too open |

For "permission denied", check in order: that you are using the right user name, that the right key is being offered (shown by `-v`), that the public key is in `authorized_keys` on the server, and that the permissions of the home directory, `.ssh` and `authorized_keys` on the server are strict. The server's own log, in `/var/log/auth.log` or the journal, states the reason exactly.

steps.title: The changed key
steps.text: An engineer connects to `web01` as they do every day, and SSH prints "WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED" and refuses. A colleague suggests deleting `~/.ssh/known_hosts`.

steps.title: Exercise: set up access
steps.text:

Write the steps to create your key and get it installed, the `~/.ssh/config` that lets you type `ssh app01` and `ssh db01`, and a command that copies a local file `dump.sql` to `/tmp` on `db01`. Then name three things you would not do.

steps.text:
**Key**


The administrator adds that one line to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` for `ana` on each machine.

**Config**


**Copy the file**


`scp` reads the same config, so the jump through the bastion happens by itself.

**Three things not to do**

1. **Send the private key to anyone, or copy it onto the bastion.** `ProxyJump` exists so that the key never leaves the laptop.
2. **Create the key without a passphrase.** A laptop backup or a stolen file would then be a working login.
3. **Use agent forwarding to hop from the bastion.** The bastion is shared, and anyone with root there could use the forwarded agent. `ProxyJump` does the same job without that exposure.

A fourth, for later: when you leave the team, your line should be removed from `authorized_keys` on all three machines.

choices.feedback: That turns off the check that just did its job.

lessons.title: Disks, memory and load
lessons.intro: A machine has a fixed amount of disk, memory and processor. When one runs out, things fail in ways that do not always name the cause. This module covers how to measure each one and how to read the numbers.

steps.title: Disk space
steps.text:
`df` shows how full each filesystem is. `du` shows how much space a directory uses.


`-h` prints sizes in readable units. Read the `Use%` column and the `Mounted on` column. Each line is a separate filesystem, attached to the tree at that directory. Here the root filesystem is nearly full and the database's is not.

A full disk causes failures that look unrelated: a service that will not start, a database that refuses writes, a login that fails, "No space left on device" from a command that seems to write nothing. Check `df` early in any investigation.

steps.title: Finding what uses the space
steps.text:
When a filesystem is full, find the cause from the top down.


Start at the mount point, find the largest directory, and repeat inside it. Two or three rounds usually lead to the cause: logs, old releases, package caches, core dumps, container images.

`-x` (and `-xdev` for `find`) keeps the search on one filesystem. Without it, measuring `/` also counts every other disk mounted beneath it.

steps.title: Mounts
steps.text:
A **filesystem** is the structure on a disk or partition that holds files. To be used, it is **mounted**: attached to a directory in the tree, called its mount point.



This explains how one directory can be full while another has plenty of room. They are different disks. It also explains a classic accident: if a disk fails to mount, its mount point is just an empty directory on the root filesystem. A program that writes there fills the root disk, and the data vanishes from view when the real disk is mounted over it later.

steps.title: Inodes
steps.text:
A filesystem has a limit on its number of files as well as on bytes. Each file uses one **inode**, a record that holds its details, and the number of inodes is fixed when the filesystem is created.

A disk can report free space and still refuse to create a file, with "No space left on device". The cause is millions of tiny files, such as session files or a cache that is never cleaned.


When `df -h` shows room and writes still fail, run `df -i`.

steps.title: Space that does not come back
steps.text: A disk is full. An engineer finds a 40 GB log file, deletes it with `rm`, and runs `df -h`. The disk is still shown as full. The application that writes the log is still running.

steps.title: Memory
steps.text:
`free` shows how memory is used.


The real output is a little wider than shown here. The column to read is **available**, not **free**. Linux uses memory that programs do not need to keep recently read files in memory, shown as `buff/cache`. That makes disk access much faster, and the memory is handed back the moment a program asks for it.

So a low "free" figure is normal and healthy. Here only 310 MB is free, and 5.4 GB is available. This machine has plenty of memory. A machine is short of memory when "available" is low.

**Swap** is disk space used as overflow when memory runs out. Disk is thousands of times slower than memory, so a machine that is actively swapping becomes very slow. Some swap in use is harmless. Swap that keeps growing is a sign of too little memory.

steps.title: When memory runs out
steps.text:
If memory and swap are both exhausted, the kernel has to free some at once. Its **OOM killer** (out of memory) picks a process, usually the largest, and kills it with `SIGKILL`.

From the outside, a service simply disappears, with nothing in its own log, since it had no chance to write anything. The evidence is in the kernel's log.


A process that vanishes without an error should make you check for this. In containers the same thing happens when a container passes its own memory limit, and it is reported as "OOMKilled".

steps.title: Load
steps.text:
`uptime` shows how long the machine has been up and its **load average**.


The three numbers are averages over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Load is the number of processes that are running or waiting to run, and on Linux it also counts those waiting for disk.

Read it against the number of processor cores, shown by `nproc`.

- Load below the core count: there is spare capacity.
- Load about equal to the core count: fully used.
- Load well above it: work is queueing.

A load of 3.2 means nothing alone. On 4 cores it is comfortable. On 1 core it means a queue.

Compare the three numbers to see the trend. Here the load went from 0.45 to 3.20, so it is rising sharply and began within the last few minutes.

steps.title: What is the machine waiting for
steps.text:
High load has two different causes, and they need different fixes. `top` tells them apart in its summary line.


- High `us`: the processor is busy computing. Find the process using it.
- High `wa`: the processor is idle and waiting for the disk. The bottleneck is storage, and a faster processor would not help.

In this example the processor is 64% waiting for input and output. The load is high, and the cause is a slow or overloaded disk.

steps.title: A first look at any machine
steps.text:
When a machine is misbehaving, a fixed set of commands gives a picture in a minute.


Run them in this order before forming a theory. Most resource problems show up in one of these seven.

steps.title: Reading the numbers
steps.text: A 2-core server feels slow. `uptime` shows a load average of `9.50, 9.20, 8.80`. `top` shows `%Cpu(s): 4.0 us, 2.0 sy, 6.0 id, 88.0 wa`. `free -h` shows 3 GB available.

steps.title: Exercise: diagnose the server
steps.text:
At 03:10 an alert says the orders service is down. You log in and collect this.


Say what happened, citing the evidence. Explain why memory looks fine now. Say what you would do right away and what you would investigate afterwards.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**What happened.** The orders process grew until the machine ran out of memory, and the kernel's OOM killer ended it at 03:08:51.

**The evidence**

- `dmesg` says so directly: "Out of memory: Killed process 4411 (orders)". It held about 6.7 GB of the machine's 7.8 GB.
- `systemctl status` agrees: the process was killed by signal `KILL`, at the same second. A crash of its own making would show an exit code, not a kill signal.
- Swap is almost full, at 1.9 of 2.0 GB. The machine had used its overflow before it gave up.
- The load average of 2.10 over 15 minutes, against 0.30 now, shows the machine was struggling before the kill and is idle since.

**Why memory looks fine now.** The process that held it is gone. 6.4 GB is available because the cause was removed. A snapshot taken after the event shows the aftermath. The kernel log shows the event.

**Disk** is at 62% and is not involved.

**Right away.** Start the service: `sudo systemctl start orders`. Confirm that it answers. Note that it did not restart by itself, which suggests the unit has no `Restart=` policy, or that the policy does not cover a kill signal. That is worth fixing, as a mitigation only.

**Afterwards**

1. **Why did it grow?** Look at its memory over the last days in the monitoring data. A steady climb over 41 days points to a leak. A sudden jump at 03:00 points to a job or an unusually large request.
2. **What ran at about 03:00?** Check scheduled jobs and the service's own log just before 03:08.
3. **Set a memory limit** on the service (`MemoryMax=` in the unit), so that it is restarted cleanly at a known size and cannot take the whole machine with it.
4. **Alert on available memory and on swap use,** so the next occurrence is seen before the kill.

The restart is the quick fix, and it will fail again in the same way unless the growth is explained.

lessons.title: Diagnose a broken server
lessons.intro: This module has no new ideas. You work through two broken servers and review a script, using the commands from the earlier modules. Do each exercise on paper before you read its answer.

steps.title: How to use this module
steps.text:
Each exercise has a step where you work alone and a step with one possible answer. The answers are not the only good ones. Compare your reasoning with them, and pay most attention to anything you did not think of at all.

When something is wrong on a server, ask the same questions in the same order.

1. **What exactly is failing?** Get the real error message.
2. **Is the machine healthy?** Load, memory, disk.
3. **Is the service running?** Its status, and its last log lines.
4. **Can it be reached?** Listening address, port, firewall.
5. **What changed?** A deploy, an update, a configuration edit, a reboot.

Look before you change anything. A restart often makes the symptom go away and destroys the evidence of the cause.

steps.title: Case 1: the site is down
steps.text: A website returns "502 Bad Gateway". It is served by nginx on port 80, which passes requests to an application listening on port 8000. You log in and collect the following. Work out what is wrong and what you would do.

steps.title: What kind of full
steps.text: In case 1, `df -h` shows 8 GB free on `/srv`, and the application reports "No space left on device".

steps.title: Case 1: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Reading the evidence**

- nginx is running. A 502 comes from nginx itself, and means it could not get an answer from the application behind it.
- The application is in a restart loop: it starts, exits with status 1, and systemd starts it again.
- Its log gives the reason: it cannot create its PID file, "No space left on device".
- The disk has 8 GB free, and `df -i` shows that every inode is in use. The filesystem cannot hold one more file.

**Find the files**


More than a million session files, each tiny, in one directory.

**Fix**

1. Free inodes, carefully. Preview, then delete files older than a day:
   `sudo find /srv/app/tmp/sessions -type f -mtime +1 -print | head`, and then the same with `-delete`. A plain `rm *` there fails with "Argument list too long", since the shell cannot pass a million names to one command. `find` does not have that limit.
2. Check with `df -i /srv`. The application should start at its next restart attempt. Confirm with `systemctl status app` and a request with `curl`.

**Stop it from returning**

- Why are session files never removed? Add a cleanup: a timer that deletes old ones, or a session store that expires entries itself.
- Alert on inode use as well as on disk space.

**What was not the problem.** nginx, the network and the application's code. Restarting nginx, the usual first reflex for a 502, would have changed nothing.

steps.title: Case 2: cannot log in
steps.text:
A developer reports that they cannot SSH to `app02` since this morning. Others can. Yesterday they "tidied up some permissions" in their home directory on that server. They send this from their laptop, and an administrator sends the rest from the server.


Explain why the login fails, although the key is correct and `authorized_keys` has the right permissions. Write the fix. Say what the developer probably ran yesterday.

steps.title: Case 2: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Why it fails.** The client offers the right key. The server refuses to use `authorized_keys`, and its log says why: "bad ownership or modes for directory /home/dana".

The home directory is `drwxrwxrwx`, which is mode 777. Anyone on the machine can write to it. That means anyone could rename `.ssh` and put their own in its place, with their own key in it, and log in as dana. The SSH server checks for this and refuses to trust key files below a directory that others can write to. It protects the account by locking it.

The files inside are correct, which is why looking only at `.ssh` finds nothing wrong. Permissions matter along the whole path.

**Fix**, run by the administrator or through a console:


Then the developer connects again.

**What was probably run.** Something like `chmod -R 777 ~` or `chmod 777 ~`, to make a "Permission denied" go away. It is the standard wrong fix from the permissions module, and here it broke something that had worked.

**Two lessons**

- The server's log named the cause exactly. The client only ever says "Permission denied". When SSH refuses a key, read the server side.
- A more permissive mode is not always more permissive in effect. Some programs refuse to run with files that are too open: SSH with keys, and many programs with files that hold secrets.

steps.title: Review: a maintenance script
steps.text:
A team runs this from cron every night as root. Last week it deleted the application's uploads. List every fault you can find, and say which one caused the loss.


On the night of the loss, the directory named in `/etc/app/tmpdir` no longer existed. It had been removed during a configuration change, and the file still named it. The cron entry starts the script from `/srv/app`.

steps.title: The step that did the damage
steps.text: Before you read the full list, decide from the description above.

steps.title: Review: what is wrong
steps.text:
**The chain that caused the loss**

1. `TMP_DIR` held the path of a directory that had been removed.
2. `cd $TMP_DIR` failed with "No such file or directory", and the script stayed where it had started, in `/srv/app`.
3. There is no `set -e`, so the script went on to the next line.
4. `find . -mtime +7 | xargs rm -rf` deleted everything older than a week under the current directory. In `/srv/app`, that included the uploads.

**All the faults**

- No `set -euo pipefail`, so no failure stops it. With it, the failed `cd` would have ended the script.
- An empty `TMP_DIR` would be as bad: an unquoted empty value turns `cd $TMP_DIR` into plain `cd`, which goes to root's home directory.
- No check that `TMP_DIR` is set, is a directory, and is the directory expected.
- Unquoted variables.
- `find .` with a relative start. The search depends on a `cd` that may have failed.
- `find | xargs rm` breaks on names with spaces, and `-rf` hides every problem.
- No `-type f`. Whole directories older than 7 days are removed, with newer files inside them.
- `#!/bin/sh` with no assurance of which shell that is.
- It runs as root, so nothing limited what it could delete.
- `gzip *.log` compresses the log the application is writing to at that moment.
- The email says "cleanup done" whatever happened.
- Backticks work, and `$(...)` is the clearer modern form.

**Rewritten**


**What changed**

- The directory is a fixed absolute path, checked before use, and given to `find` directly. Nothing depends on the working directory.
- `-type f` and `-delete` remove files only, and handle any file name.
- Only rotated logs older than a day are compressed, and the live log is left alone.
- It should run as the application's user, not as root, so that a future mistake is limited by permissions.
- It exits non-zero on any failure, and the scheduler should alert on that.

steps.title: Where to go next
steps.text:
You can now move around a Linux system, read and search its files, join commands into pipelines, control permissions and processes, write a careful script, manage services, and work out why a machine is misbehaving.

Four habits are worth keeping.

- **Read the error message, and the log behind it.** They nearly always say what is wrong.
- **Look before you change.** Preview a pattern with `ls`, a `find` with `-print`, a `sed` without `-i`.
- **Quote your variables, and start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`.**
- **Grant the least that works.** A specific owner or group, never 777, and `sudo` only when needed.

The manual pages are the reference for everything in this course. When a command surprises you, `man` and `--help` are faster and more accurate than memory.

The Docker and CI/CD courses build directly on this one. A container is a Linux process with its own view of the filesystem and network, and a pipeline is a series of shell commands that must each exit with zero.

cleanup-fixed.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

tmp_dir="/srv/app/tmp"

if [ ! -d "$tmp_dir" ]; then
  echo "cleanup: $tmp_dir is not a directory" >&2
  exit 1
fi

find "$tmp_dir" -xdev -type f -mtime +7 -delete

find /var/log/app -name "*.log.*" ! -name "*.gz" -mtime +1 \
  -exec gzip {} +

echo "cleanup ok"
